title: Day 1 · Phase 1 — Re-anchoring: the bridge to the Car Project + meet electric charge
bodyHtml:
DAY 1 · Phase 1 — Setting up the question

Unit 7 is the last theory unit before Unit 8's Car Project. Every part of that build — battery, switch, motor, wiring — is in this unit.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS (preview)

K1. Electric charge as the fundamental quantity. R1. Why opposite charges attract; like repel.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used wave and signal models to interpret observations of the fictional asteroid. This unit connects electric and magnetic interactions to instruments, powered systems, and the vehicle capstone.

How today connects:

end of Unit 6. Radar told us the asteroid. Now Unit 7 closes the theory year by getting us to electrical+magnetic phenomena AT planetary AND human scales.

Today's pivot: Two threads converge in Unit 7. (1) Earth's magnetosphere protects us from cosmic + solar radiation — large impacts CAN disrupt it. (2) Unit 8's Car Project literally builds a circuit. Today through Day 15: the foundations. Day 16: asteroid/cosmic E&M. Day 17: the explicit bridge into the Car Project.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Return Unit 6 transfer tasks. Highlight strong radar reasoning. "Now we trade waves for charges. Two weeks of theory, then we BUILD."

5–18 min

• Demo: rub a balloon on hair. Stick to wall. Why? Then: tear paper into bits, sprinkle. Bring the rubbed balloon near. Bits jump up. Force without contact. What's happening?

18–28 min

• Notice & Wonder. Push toward: there's a PROPERTY (call it charge) that comes in TWO KINDS, and they pull on each other through space. Don't define yet — just name it.

28–42 min

• Mini-lecture preview: Unit 7's payoffs. (1) Days 4-10: circuits — voltage, current, resistance, series + parallel — everything the Car Project needs. (2) Days 12-15: magnetism + electromagnetism — Oersted, Faraday, motors. (3) Day 16: planetary-scale E&M (magnetosphere + EMP scenarios). (4) Day 17: explicit bridge into Unit 8.

42–48 min

• Individual exit: Two balloons each gain electrons when rubbed with wool. What net charge does each balloon have, what charge is left on the wool, and what happens when the balloons approach each other? Explain using electron transfer, charge conservation and the rule for like charges.

48–50 min

• Marzano on K1 preview.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Compare the initial prediction with the observed attraction and repulsion. Students should explain charge transfer without claiming that rubbing creates net charge from nothing.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: Unit 6 transfer tasks scored; balloons + hair (hand sanitizer can help when hair fails); torn paper bits; whiteboard with two columns for student observations.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 32 §32.1. Honors: Ch 32 §32.1, 32.2, 32.4.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §18.1 Static Electricity and Charge: Conservation of Charge (pp. 833–837); §18.2 Conductors and Insulators (pp. 838–841). Focus: Distinguish charge from current; use charge conservation and conductor/insulator models. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on "why two kinds of charge": resist explaining. Push: "What would happen if all charges were the same kind? Could anything ever attract or stick?"

Differentiation: ELs — visual showing balloon-on-hair triboelectric pattern with +/- annotated; SWDs — verbal exit ticket option; Honors extension — "could you have a UNIVERSE with one kind of charge instead of two? Why does ours have two?"

CPA teaching sequence: Begin with an actual low-voltage setup or labeled circuit diagram. Trace one complete path, label known quantities, model one reduction or equation move per line, then guide a parallel example before independent work.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

title: Day 2 · Phase 2 — Coulomb's law: F = kq₁q₂/r²
bodyHtml:
DAY 2 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

F = k·q₁q₂/r². Inverse-square law for charges, structurally identical to gravity.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K2. Coulomb's law structure. S1. Compute Coulomb force.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used wave and signal models to interpret observations of the fictional asteroid. This unit connects electric and magnetic interactions to instruments, powered systems, and the vehicle capstone. The preceding meeting focused on Re-anchoring: the bridge to the Car Project + meet electric charge.

How today connects:

Compare Coulomb's law (F = k·q₁q₂/r²) to Newton's universal gravitation (F = G·m₁m₂/r²). Same structure. Different constants, different scaled outcomes. Both inverse-square. Why does physics keep doing this?

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Hand back Day 1 exit tickets. Anchor: "Today we get the equation."

5–18 min

• Direct instruction: F = k·q₁q₂/r². k = 9×10⁹ N·m²/C². Units of q = Coulombs (C). Compare to Newton's gravity — SAME STRUCTURE. But k is HUGE (gravity's G is tiny) → electrical force is much stronger at small distances.

18–30 min

• Worked example 1: F between two 1-C charges 1 m apart. F = 9×10⁹ N. Stunning number. Why we never see 1 C of net charge in everyday life.

30–42 min

• Worked example 2: F between two electrons (q = -1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C each) at 10⁻¹⁰ m (atomic scale). Compare to gravitational F between two electron masses at the same distance. Electrical is ~10⁴² times stronger.

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "If you DOUBLE the distance between two charges, what happens to F?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on K2/S1.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check charge units, squared separation, and the attractive or repulsive direction. Students should reason about sign separately from the magnitude calculation.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: packet practice; calculator; reference table comparing gravity vs. Coulomb constants.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 32 §32.3. Honors: Ch 32 §32.3 + Think and Solve 47, 48.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §18.4 Coulomb’s Law (pp. 846–848). Focus: Apply inverse-square reasoning to electric forces and track charge signs separately from force magnitude. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on "why we never see 1 C of charge": push: "What kind of force WOULD it take to assemble 1 C? Why does electrostatic repulsion fight against you?"

Differentiation: ELs — equation card with each piece labeled; SWDs — pre-built table for the two-side-by-side comparison (gravity vs. Coulomb); Honors extension — "compute the ratio of Coulomb to gravitational force between two protons. Why is gravity dominant at galaxy scales but Coulomb dominant at human scales?"

title: Day 3 · Phase 2 — Electric field (qualitative)
bodyHtml:
DAY 3 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

E = F/q. Field lines point from + to −. Vector field that fills space around charges.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K3. Electric field as F per unit charge. Field-line direction conventions.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used wave and signal models to interpret observations of the fictional asteroid. This unit connects electric and magnetic interactions to instruments, powered systems, and the vehicle capstone. The preceding meeting focused on Coulomb's law: F = kq₁q₂/r².

How today connects:

Just like Unit 2's gravitational field g(r), today we define E(r) — the electric field around a charge. The field is the FRAMEWORK both gravity and electricity share.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Recap Coulomb's law: F = k·q₁q₂/r².

5–18 min

• Direct instruction: divide both sides by q_test. Define E = F/q. Units: N/C. The electric field is the FORCE PER UNIT CHARGE that a tiny positive test charge would feel.

18–30 min

• Field lines: arrows pointing in the direction of force on a positive test charge. Field lines START on + charges and END on − charges. Diagram on the board: single +, single −, dipole, parallel plates.

30–42 min

• PhET Charges and Fields sim: place a charge, watch the field. Add another. See the dipole pattern. Place a test charge and watch it move.

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "Draw the field lines for a single negative charge. Which way do they point?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on K3.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Look for electric-field direction defined by a positive test charge. Field lines do not cross because the field has one direction at a given point.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: PhET Charges and Fields loaded on lab computers; field-line drawing template for the board.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 33 §33.1. Honors: Ch 33 §33.1–33.3 + Think and Solve 36, 38.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §18.5 Electric Field: Concept of a Field Revisited (pp. 848–850); §18.6 Electric Field Lines: Multiple Charges (pp. 850–853). Focus: Define electric field with a positive test charge and read field direction and relative strength from diagrams. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on "field lines point AWAY from + and TOWARD −": when students get confused, push: "What direction would a tiny POSITIVE charge be pushed? That's the direction the lines point."

Differentiation: ELs — pre-drawn field-line patterns with direction arrows; SWDs — drawing template for single +/− and dipole; Honors extension — "explain why field lines NEVER cross. Hint: what would happen to a test charge at a crossing?"

title: Day 4 · Phase 2 — Voltage: electrical potential difference
bodyHtml:
DAY 4 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

V = U/q. Volts = Joules/Coulomb. Voltage is what PUSHES current through a wire.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K4. Voltage as potential difference.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used wave and signal models to interpret observations of the fictional asteroid. This unit connects electric and magnetic interactions to instruments, powered systems, and the vehicle capstone. The preceding meeting focused on Electric field (qualitative).

How today connects:

The Car Project uses a 9V battery. The voltage is what pushes current through the motor. Today we untangle what "voltage" really means.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Hook: "AA battery is 1.5 V. Car battery is 12 V. House outlet is 120 V. What does the number MEAN?"

5–18 min

• Direct instruction: V = U/q. Voltage is energy per unit charge. 1 V = 1 J of energy delivered per 1 C of charge that passes. The voltage of a battery tells you how much PUSH (energy per charge) it provides.

18–30 min

• Water analogy: voltage = water pressure. Tall tank (high voltage) pushes water harder than short tank. The battery is like a pump that keeps the "water" (charge) pushed up to a height.

30–42 min

• Worked examples: (1) 9V battery delivers 1.5 C of charge through a motor. How much energy delivered? (13.5 J) (2) How much charge has to flow through a 1.5V battery to deliver 1 J of energy? (0.67 C)

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "A battery does 60 J of work pushing 5 C of charge through a circuit. What's the battery voltage?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on K4.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check volts as joules per coulomb. Students must distinguish potential difference from current and identify the two points being compared.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: AA + 9V + lithium-ion battery props; water-tank analogy diagram; packet practice; calculator.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 33 §33.5. Honors: Ch 33 §33.4–33.6 + Think and Solve 35, 39, 40.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §19.1 Electric Potential Energy: Potential Difference (pp. 881–886). Focus: Explain potential difference as energy transferred per unit charge; distinguish voltage from force and current. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on the water analogy: push: "What's the analog of CURRENT in the water analogy? What's RESISTANCE?" (Preview tomorrow.)

Differentiation: ELs — analogy card (voltage = pressure, current = flow, resistance = pipe-narrowness); SWDs — pre-built unit-conversion practice (V → J/C and back); Honors extension — "why does a 9V battery NOT shock you, but a 120V outlet might? Voltage isn't the only factor — preview tomorrow."

title: Day 5 · Phase 2 — Current: I = q/t
bodyHtml:
DAY 5 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

I = q/t. Amperes = Coulombs/second. Current is how many charges per second flow past a point.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K5. Current definition.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used wave and signal models to interpret observations of the fictional asteroid. This unit connects electric and magnetic interactions to instruments, powered systems, and the vehicle capstone. The preceding meeting focused on Voltage: electrical potential difference.

How today connects:

The Car Project's motor needs a CURRENT — flowing charge through the motor coil makes it spin. Today's foundation, applied tomorrow as Ohm's law.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Recap voltage as energy/charge.

5–18 min

• Direct instruction: current I = q/t. Units: amperes (A) = Coulombs/second. 1 A is HUGE — it's ~6×10¹⁸ electrons per second. Conventional current direction: + to − (historical; electrons actually flow − to +).

18–30 min

• Worked example: 10 A flowing for 3 s — how much charge? 30 C. 60 C passes in a minute — what current? 1 A. A 9V battery rated at 1000 mAh — how many hours at 1 A continuous draw? (1 hour.)

30–42 min

• Direction of conventional current (+ → −) AND direction of electron motion (− → +). Important for Day 13 (Oersted's right-hand rule).

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "A 9V battery rated at 500 mAh: how many hours can it provide 0.5 A?" (Use I·t = charge.)

48–50 min

• Marzano on K5.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check amperes as coulombs per second and a complete conducting path. Conventional current and electron motion have opposite directions in metal wires.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: battery with mAh ratings shown; reference table (amp = C/s); packet practice; calculator.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 34 §34.2. Honors: Ch 34 §34.1–34.3 + Think and Solve 59, 60.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §20.1 Current (pp. 925–930). Focus: Connect current with charge flow per time; distinguish conventional current from electron drift. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on conventional vs. electron current: when students get confused, stop. "There are two conventions. We use 'conventional' (+ → −) for circuit math. Just know they're opposite to electron flow."

Differentiation: ELs — water-flow visual showing pressure (V), pipe (R), flow rate (I); SWDs — pre-built I·t = q practice; Honors extension — "explain mAh in terms of Coulombs. (mAh is just an energy-related unit — it's charge.)"

title: Day 6 · Phase 2 — Ohm's law: V = IR
bodyHtml:
DAY 6 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

V = IR. Resistance in Ohms (Ω). The triangle that EVERY circuit problem leans on.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K6. Ohm's law. S2. Compute V = IR.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used wave and signal models to interpret observations of the fictional asteroid. This unit connects electric and magnetic interactions to instruments, powered systems, and the vehicle capstone. The preceding meeting focused on Current: I = q/t.

How today connects:

The Car Project's motor has resistance — that determines how much current the 9V battery can push through. Today's V = IR is THE equation for Unit 8.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Recap voltage + current. What CONNECTS them?

5–18 min

• Direct instruction: V = IR. R = resistance, measured in Ohms (Ω) = V/A. Big R = less current for same voltage. Small R = more current. Wire = ~0 Ω. Light bulb filament = a few Ω. A 1-kΩ resistor restricts current heavily.

18–32 min

• Worked examples: (1) 9V across a 100 Ω resistor — I = ? (90 mA) (2) A bulb with 2 Ω resistance carries 6 A — what voltage drove it? (12V) (3) 5 mA through a component when 1.5V across — resistance? (300 Ω)

32–42 min

• Pattern: Ohm's law triangle (V on top, I and R on bottom). Cover V to find V = IR. Cover I to find I = V/R. Cover R to find R = V/I. Master this triangle.

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "A circuit has 12V across a 4 Ω resistor. What's the current?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on K6/S2.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check which of V, I, and R is unknown and whether the equation has been rearranged before substitution. State the ohmic model rather than assume every device has constant resistance.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: Ohm's law triangle for the board; packet practice; calculator availability; sample resistors for prop.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 34 §34.5. Honors: Ch 34 §34.4–34.6 + Think and Solve 61, 67.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §20.2 Ohm’s Law: Resistance and Simple Circuits (pp. 931–933); §20.3 Resistance and Resistivity (pp. 934–936). Focus: Apply Ohm's law to an ohmic component and explain how material and geometry affect resistance. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on the triangle: have students PRACTICE rearranging out loud. "Voltage = current × resistance. Current = voltage / resistance. Resistance = voltage / current."

Differentiation: ELs — Ohm's law triangle on a card; SWDs — pre-built table for the three forms; Honors extension — "why does a thin wire have MORE resistance than a thick wire of the same material? Hint: cross-sectional area."

title: Day 7 · Phase 2 — Series circuits
bodyHtml:
DAY 7 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Series: components share the same current. Voltages ADD. Resistances ADD.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K7. Series circuit rules. S3. Solve series problems.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used wave and signal models to interpret observations of the fictional asteroid. This unit connects electric and magnetic interactions to instruments, powered systems, and the vehicle capstone. The preceding meeting focused on Ohm's law: V = IR.

How today connects:

The Car Project's circuit IS a series circuit. Battery → switch → motor → battery. Today's rules apply directly on Day 17.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Recap V = IR.

5–18 min

• Direct instruction: in a series circuit (one loop), every component sees the SAME current. The voltage drops across each component ADD to equal the battery's voltage (Kirchhoff voltage law). Resistances ADD: R_total = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ + ...

18–32 min

• Worked examples: (1) 12V battery + 2Ω + 4Ω in series. Total R = 6Ω. Current = 2A. Voltage across each: 4V + 8V = 12V ✓. (2) Three identical bulbs in series at 12V: each gets 4V.

32–42 min

• Group practice — 4 problems. Build series circuits in PhET Circuit Construction Kit. Measure I and V at each component. Confirm rules.

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "A 9V battery is in series with a 2 Ω and a 4 Ω resistor. What's the current? What's the voltage across the 4 Ω?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on K7/S3.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Look for one current through a series loop and voltage drops summing to the source. An open switch stops the current throughout that loop.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: PhET Circuit Construction Kit: DC loaded; packet practice; calculator availability; battery + resistors + bulbs + wires + multimeters for hands-on if available.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 35 §35.3. Honors: Ch 35 §35.1–35.3 + Think and Solve 48, 49.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §21.1 Resistors in Series and Parallel (pp. 974–977). Focus: Read Resistors in Series only; explain the common current and voltage division. Stop at Resistors in Parallel. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on "same current": push: "Why is the current the SAME at every point in a series loop? Where would extra charges PILE UP if it weren't?" (Charge conservation — no, it can't.)

title: Day 8 · Phase 2 — Parallel circuits
bodyHtml:
DAY 8 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Parallel: branches share the same voltage. Currents ADD. 1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ...

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K7. Parallel circuit rules. S3. Solve parallel problems.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used wave and signal models to interpret observations of the fictional asteroid. This unit connects electric and magnetic interactions to instruments, powered systems, and the vehicle capstone. The preceding meeting focused on Series circuits.

How today connects:

House wiring is parallel — that's why one light burning out doesn't take down the whole house. Day 17 contrast: Car Project is series — one wire break stops everything.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Quick check: series rules.

5–18 min

• Direct instruction: parallel = multiple paths. Each branch sees the SAME voltage (= battery voltage). Currents in each branch ADD to total. Resistances: 1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ...

18–32 min

• Worked example: 12V across two parallel 6Ω resistors. Each branch carries 12/6 = 2A. Total = 4A. R_total = 12V/4A = 3Ω (matches 1/R_total = 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 = 1/3).

32–42 min

• Group practice — 4 parallel problems. Use PhET. Note: ADDING a parallel branch DECREASES total resistance (more paths for current).

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "Three 6 Ω resistors in parallel — what's the total resistance?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on K7/S3.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check equal voltage across parallel branches and total current as the sum of branch currents. Adding a conducting branch lowers equivalent resistance.

30–42 min

• Energy usage: a 100W bulb on for 10 hours uses 1 kWh. That's what you're billed for. 1 kWh ≈ 3.6×10⁶ J.

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "A heater draws 12 A at 240V. What's its power? What energy does it use in 2 hours?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on K8/S4.

TimeWhat happens

• Recap Oersted: current makes B-field. Today: REVERSE — changing B-field makes current.

• Demo: coil + multimeter (or galvanometer). Move a bar magnet in and out. Watch the meter deflect.

30–42 min

• Applications: generators (mechanical motion → electrical energy). Transformers (changing currents → induced voltage). Wireless charging (oscillating magnetic field → AC in receiver coil).

42–48 min

48–50 min

This unit connects electric and magnetic interactions to instruments, powered systems, and the vehicle capstone. The preceding meeting focused on Motors + generators: the Car Project's heart.

How today connects:

Earth's magnetosphere protects life by deflecting solar wind. An asteroid impact ionizes the atmosphere — creating a brief but powerful electromagnetic disturbance. Plus: the magnetic field has measurable changes from past large impacts.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Frame: "Earth has its own magnetic field. Why does it matter for our story?"

5–18 min

Magnetosphere: Earth’s magnetic field interacts with charged particles from the solar wind. Mars lacks a global magnetic field today; solar wind and radiation contribute to atmospheric escape. Do not reduce the different histories of the two atmospheres to a single cause.

18–32 min

Apply induction to a hypothetical engineering scenario: a changing magnetic field links a conducting loop. Draw the loop, indicate how flux changes, and predict whether an emf is induced. Discuss what evidence would be needed before claiming that a particular asteroid impact produces damaging electromagnetic effects at a distance.

32–42 min

Discussion: compare two modeled conductor-loop geometries under the same changing magnetic field. Identify the flux change and the closed path. Keep the induction explanation separate from an unsupported claim about damage to a grid or satellite.

42–48 min

Individual exit: Explain why a changing flux through a loop can induce an emf while a stationary field need not. Name one measurement you would need before applying that model to an asteroid-impact scenario.

48–50 min

• Marzano on R4.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check that students distinguish established field/induction mechanisms from a speculative impact scenario. Ask which changing fields and conducting paths their explanation requires.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: magnetosphere diagram; aurora image; reference to nuclear-test EMP history.

Hewitt reading: CPA: no reading. Honors: Ch 36 §36.9, 36.6.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, revisit §23.2 Faraday’s Law of Induction: Lenz’s Law (pp. 1083–1086); §22.3 Magnetic Fields and Magnetic Field Lines (pp. 1035–1036). Focus: Use induction for the explicitly hypothetical field-change model. Consult the course sources for Earth's magnetosphere; these excerpts do not establish impact-driven grid damage. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves: require a cause-and-effect chain with a specified changing field, loop geometry, and conducting path. Ionized material alone is not evidence of a large coherent current or a distant damaging pulse.

Differentiation: ELs — visual of magnetosphere deflecting solar wind; SWDs — pre-printed cause-effect chart for EMP; Honors extension — "why are SHORT electrical wires less vulnerable to EMP than LONG ones?"

CPA teaching sequence: Begin with an actual low-voltage setup or labeled circuit diagram. Trace one complete path, label known quantities, model one reduction or equation move per line, then guide a parallel example before independent work.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

Collect the individual evidence before the 1–3 target self-rating. Use the evidence to choose the next teaching step; completion, video viewing, and a student self-rating do not set a teacher mastery rating.

Teacher reference: NASA Mars facts and MAVEN atmospheric-loss findings. Distinguish measured planetary evidence from the hypothetical impact extension.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

Set the assessment conditions: individual work; calculator and the agreed equation/constants card allowed. Clarifying questions are welcome; physics-content coaching and new video help wait until after the assessment.

5–15 min

Read the task silently. Record what you notice and wonder. Clarify the meaning of the prompt and supplied data without discussing a solution.

15–25 min

Plan the work against Science / Reasoning / Communication / Transfer-to-Asteroid. Identify the needed diagrams, equations, evidence, units, assumptions, and public-facing explanation.

25–45 min

Begin the task independently. The teacher records approaches and access needs without giving content help.

45–50 min

Record the next step and the dimension that needs attention. Hand in work in progress for safekeeping; retrieve it at the next meeting. The task stays in class.

TRANSFER TASK

• Transfer task. Independent. 5 multi-part problems: (1) Coulomb's law — F between two charges; (2) Ohm's law on a 6V battery + resistor; (3) combination circuit reduction + branch currents; (4) electric power + energy (kWh); (5) Car Project circuit — use a specified resistive-load model to compute current, power, and charge over 30 seconds; explain why a running motor requires measured operating data.

Public-facing transfer: Use the circuit analysis to explain one design choice for a powered response to 2026-XJ. Compare it with the model vehicle and name a limit of that comparison.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check the independent task plan for circuit topology, units, model limits, and all four rubric dimensions. Provide task clarification without calculating a branch current.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

Materials and setup: transfer task printed; calculators; constants reference card (k, conventions); quiet testing environment; growth chart pages.

Two-meeting assessment: This is the first of two full class periods. Day 19 is for completion, peer defense, final revision, and submission. The preceding synthesis lesson is retained.

Assessment conventions: Use the Unit 1 rubric: Science / Reasoning / Communication / Transfer-to-Asteroid. Score the four dimensions independently from 0–4; report the profile without averaging and use the established lowest-dimension conversion. Science checks the physics; Reasoning checks the choice and justification of the model; Communication checks labeled, organized work; Transfer-to-Asteroid checks the supported connection and its limits. Peer and student ratings are feedback; the teacher makes the final judgment. Target self-ratings use the separate 1–3 scale and do not automatically become mastery ratings. Revisions follow Unit 1’s two-week window, with new evidence for a one-level move on a dimension.

CPA access: Supply agreed labeled diagrams or vector components when component derivation is not the assessed target. Keep the same physics prompt and rubric; Honors students can justify or derive the corresponding model.
